files.name: 2026-08-11.md

frontmatter.title: The first commit, and beats become scenes

files.body:
Put the Worldbuilder codebase under version control and immediately tore out the first thing that
wasn't working.

The Story Planner had a beats checklist — tick a box when your story hits a beat. It looked useful
and taught me nothing. A checklist tells you whether something happened; it can't tell you whether
the scene is doing any work. Replaced it with a structured scene-and-sequel model, which asks what
the character wants going in, what stops them, and what they decide as a result. Harder to fill in,
which is the point. A form you can complete without thinking is a form that isn't asking anything.

Also fixed a scene modal you couldn't scroll to the bottom of — a self-inflicted wound, since the
fields I'd just added were the ones out of reach — and made chapters reorderable by dragging.

Starting a log on day one of version control feels like the right moment, even though the app is a
few months old by now. Everything before this exists only as a working directory.

files.name: 2026-08-12.md

frontmatter.title: Search that finds the thing you meant

files.body:
Chapter search in the Manuscript Spine, and a fix for Jots content search that had been matching
titles but not bodies.

Small day. Search is one of those features nobody praises and everybody notices when it's missing, or
worse, when it's there and quietly wrong. A search that returns nothing looks identical to a search
for something that isn't there.

files.name: 2026-08-13.md

frontmatter.title: Scene cards that say how a scene connects

files.body:
Extended the scene card to record three things I'd been keeping in my head: how a scene connects to
the one before it, whether it charges the story positively or negatively, and what kind of
cliffhanger it ends on.

The connector is the one I care about most. A sequence of scenes that are each fine on their own can
still read as a list, and the reason is almost always that nothing in scene four needs scene three
to have happened. Making the connection an explicit field means the gap shows up while I'm planning
rather than on a reread three chapters later.

The rest of the day was making sure those fields don't die in the form. A field you fill in once and
never see again is worse than no field — it costs you the effort and returns nothing. So they now
surface in the scene export and in the writing guide that sits beside the manuscript while I draft,
and the guide shows every scene card field rather than a curated few, with a minimize toggle for
when I want the screen back.

Also made the manuscript sidebar collapsible, which is a small thing that matters on a laptop.

files.name: 2026-08-14.md

frontmatter.title: The app became something I can use on a phone

files.body:
Twenty commits taking the app from desktop-only to an installable phone app, ending at v2.0.0. Six
phases: the install shell, then the layout, then the easy workspaces, then dragging, then the hard
canvases — the relation graph, the timeline, the story planner.

Two bugs worth keeping.

Dropping an event on the timeline landed it years away from where I released it. The drop was being
measured against the wrong thing, and on a phone — where the whole gesture is your thumb covering
the target — it was unusable rather than merely annoying.

The second one cost me the most and taught me the most. Any modal opened from a mobile pane was
dead: it painted perfectly and swallowed every tap. The pane marks the rest of the app inert so
touches can't leak through, and the browser then excludes that whole region from hit testing — so
the modal drawn inside it was visible and untouchable. Everything now goes through one shared modal
that escapes the pane entirely. I'd have found this in ten minutes on a device and spent an hour
looking at it in a desktop browser at phone width.

Also took the chance to fix two things I'd have defended if asked: a timing guess where a real
measurement belonged, and styles being injected at runtime into the editor.

The standing rule out of today is that mobile isn't a follow-up. If a change only works on desktop,
it's half-done.

files.name: 2026-08-15.md

frontmatter.title: What shipping to a phone actually revealed

files.body:
The biggest day so far, and it started with three bugs that only exist once something is genuinely
installed rather than merely responsive.

Signing in with Google inside the installed app bounced you straight back to the login screen. The
service worker — the thing that makes it work offline — only registered after sign-in, so a first
visit got none of it. And the page itself was being cached for an hour, which meant shipping a fix
and watching people keep the old one. None of these can be found on localhost. You have to install
the thing and use it.

Then a long stretch of making the manuscript editor feel like a manuscript editor: book typography
with a draft/page toggle, dialogue tools that do curly quotes and new-speaker line breaks properly,
export to .docx and Markdown, autocorrect, and find-and-replace.

The part I'm most glad about is less visible. I added a test harness and wrote the first real tests,
made the app degrade to local storage instead of half-dying when Firebase can't start, and fixed
backups that didn't actually contain the project — which is a terrifying sentence to write about a
feature named backup. Then I broke the largest component into pieces and deleted AI Loom outright.

Deleting AI Loom was the right call. It generated prose. I don't want an app that writes for me; I
want one that notices things about what I wrote. Everything I built afterwards — the Chekhov ledger
that pairs setups with payoffs, character arcs, the scene rhythm strip, prose diagnostics for echoed
words and filter words — follows from that. They tell me things and never touch the text.

files.name: 2026-08-16.md

frontmatter.title: Magic systems got their own category

files.body:
Two themes today: making the app easier to extend, and then immediately using that to add the thing
I'd been faking.

The extensibility work first — one registry for local-mode collections instead of the same list
copied in several places, the sprawling Analysis Hub split into per-tab panels, and form fields
described by the schema rather than hand-built one at a time. Boring, and it paid for itself within
hours.

Because then: Systems. Magic, technology, whatever set of rules your world runs on. I'd previously
handled this with four fixed fields bolted onto a scene, which was a guess about what a system is
that turned out to be wrong for every system I actually wrote. Now a system is a first-class thing
you can define, and a scene records which ones it invokes. Existing data migrates itself, once,
without asking.

I also changed how this project ships. Previously every phase got its own version and release. That
meant releasing things I hadn't looked at together, which is how you find out two features are fine
alone and contradictory side by side. Now a group of phases ends at a gate, and only gates ship.

Ended the day starting in-world calendars, so a story can have its own months and its own year
count rather than pretending everything happens in ours.

Also shipped: a global search palette, margin comments on the manuscript, and writing history with
targets.

files.name: 2026-08-17.md

frontmatter.title: Fifty-four commits, and one feature deleted

files.body:
The longest day on this project. Four release gates, v2.11.0 through v2.15.0.

The Continuity Audit landed, with four checks that know when to shut up — a check that fires on every
scene gets ignored, so each one has conditions under which it stays quiet. Alongside it, dual
ordering, so the Storyboard reads in either narrative or chronological order.

Then progressions: how an entity changes over time, with a resolver to ask what something looked like
at a given point, and a stated rule for mixed indexing. That made the dead-character-speaking check
possible, which is exactly the kind of error you don't catch by rereading.

More in the same day — typed relationships and four layout modes for the Relation Graph, nested maps
and layers on the Lore Maps canvas, custom fields per lore category, three new categories, entity
templates, an unwritten-entity worklist, unlinked mentions, location mood boards, EPUB export,
read-aloud, chapter word-count targets, accessibility controls, Markdown and .docx import, and
project-wide restore checkpoints built on word-level snapshot diffs.

Two things I'd point at rather than the volume.

I ran a fix wave — a deliberate pass through review findings, rather than fixing things as I tripped
over them. The critical one: code was setting a key to undefined instead of omitting it, which
Firestore treats very differently from the local mock.

And I deleted Lore Maps entirely, three commits after building more of it that same day. Code, docs
and stray references. It was a feature I wanted rather than one the app needed, and keeping it would
have meant maintaining a second canvas forever. Also deleted the Character Dashboard, folding it into
Lore Explorer so there's one character editor instead of two that drift apart.

files.name: 2026-08-18.md

frontmatter.title: Letting someone read the book without an account

files.body:
Two gates, v2.16.0 and v2.17.0. The first was sharing, which is the first feature in this app that
lets anyone other than me see anything.

That made it the first feature where being wrong is expensive. A share link opens a read-only view
with no account required, so everything about it had to be built assuming the reader is a stranger:
a separate, deliberately narrow set of rules for what public data can be touched, and a sanitiser
that strips anything not meant to leave. It refuses links whose destination it can't vouch for
rather than passing them through, and I proved the rules against a local emulator instead of
trusting that they read correctly. Readers can leave feedback, which lands in the same worklist as
my own margin comments — one place to look, not two.

Alongside it, series support: several books sharing one codex of characters and places, so an entity
can belong to the series rather than to a single book. A share can then cover one book or the whole
series.

The second gate was help. The app had grown far more fields than anyone could guess the meaning of,
including me on a bad day. Rather than write help text twice, the in-app help is generated from the
reference document I already maintain, so there's no second copy to drift. Every field can carry a
small "?" that explains itself in place.

Also settled that the name is Worldbuilder, one word, everywhere. It had been spelled three ways.

files.name: 2026-08-19.md

frontmatter.title: The bug that hid every piece of feedback

files.body:
Wrote help text and proper labels for the fields across every category, which is unglamorous and was
overdue — a form full of terms only I understand is a form only I can fill in.

Then a density pass on mobile. The phone layout had been a direct translation of the desktop one,
which meant enormous headings, padding sized for a mouse, and about a third of the screen doing
nothing. Tighter type, edge-to-edge panes, denser lists.

The bug of the day was the worst kind. Reader feedback on a shared link was arriving and being stored
correctly, and the worklist showed nothing at all. Not an error, not an empty state that admitted
uncertainty — just a clean, confident "no feedback". The query needed an index that didn't exist, so
it failed quietly and the screen reported the failure as an answer. Anyone who'd left me notes on the
manuscript would have assumed I'd read them and ignored them.

That's the shape of failure I keep meeting on this project: something breaks and the interface fills
the gap with a plausible-looking nothing. A visible error is always better.

Also made local mode reject the same bad writes that the real database rejects. They'd been diverging,
which meant testing locally could pass while the live version quietly refused — the exact thing local
mode exists to prevent.

Two follow-up fixes after that: mobile layers opening behind the sheet that spawned them, and a
calendar day field that would run away from you as you typed.

files.name: 2026-08-20.md

frontmatter.title: Nobody should have to paste a UUID

files.body:
Two releases, both fixing places where the app made me do its work for it.

The first was dates. Entering an in-world date meant typing numbers into boxes, which is slow and
wrong often enough to be irritating. Now you tap a calendar and a clock, in your own world's months.
Scenes can also carry a date relative to another scene — "three days after the funeral" — because
that's how I actually think about chronology while drafting. Absolute dates come later, if ever.

The second was worse and had been there a long time. Linking one entity to another meant pasting its
unique id, a string of random characters, into a field. I'd built it that way early on because it was
easy to build, and then I got used to it — which is the part that bothers me. I stopped noticing that
the app was asking me to look up an internal identifier and copy it by hand. You now type the name.

Both are the same lesson from different angles: the app should meet me where I'm thinking. If I'm
thinking about a funeral three days ago, or about a character named Elias, that's what I should be
able to type.

files.name: 2026-08-23.md

frontmatter.title: Fields that link instead of describing

files.body:
Four releases, all about the same complaint: the app kept asking me to write out things it already
knew.

Eight fields that had been free text — the sort of thing where you type a character's name into a
box about another character — now link to the actual entity. Once they link, the connection works in
both directions and shows up everywhere that entity appears, instead of being a name I typed that
happens to match. The version where you describe a relationship in prose looks equivalent and gives
you nothing back.

Also: a Reference Panel that keeps the same shape whichever entity you open, rather than rearranging
itself depending on which fields happen to be filled. That instability made it useless for glancing
at, which is its entire job. And a Lore Explorer that finally uses the width of a desktop screen
instead of one narrow column with acres of grey either side.

One fix I'd call an admission rather than a bug. The Storyboard's opening field was labelled Goal,
and I'd been filling it with a description of the scene every single time. Rather than train myself,
I relabelled it to what everyone was actually using it for. When the whole user base gets a field
wrong the same way, the field is wrong.

files.name: 2026-08-24.md

frontmatter.title: Killing a character became something the app knows about

files.body:
Character death, properly modelled. Until today a character dying was just something that happened in
the prose, which meant nothing downstream could know about it — the app would happily let a dead
character speak eleven chapters later and say nothing.

Now a death is pinned to the scene it happens in. Mark it from the writing guide or the storyboard,
undo it if the draft changes its mind, and there's a read-only status ledger showing who's alive, who
isn't, and where it happened. Because it's pinned to a scene rather than set as a flag, it moves
correctly when scenes get reordered, which they constantly do.

Three defects turned up in the logic before it shipped and one after — a retry could leave the record
half-written, orphaning the death from the character. Worth saying plainly: I found those by writing
tests for the reasoning before wiring any of it to a button. The alternative is discovering it in
December when a ledger tells me someone's alive who died in chapter nine.

Earlier in the day, a release making the writing guide something you open when you want it, with an
explicit End Scene, and Write Scene taking you to the scene rather than the top of the chapter.

Also pinned the mobile manuscript box above the keyboard toolbar. Typing on a phone and watching your
own sentence disappear behind the keyboard is the kind of thing that makes you close the app.

files.name: 2026-08-25.md

frontmatter.title: Stopped losing edits I had not saved

files.body:
Nine commits, two releases, v2.28.0 and v2.29.0.

The whole day was one theme: the app was throwing away work. Switching tabs or chapters discarded
pending manuscript edits. Leaving the Lore Explorer with unsaved changes lost them silently.

Fixed both. Added a dirty-tracking layer to the lore form with an "Unsaved changes" pill, and made
leaving park the edits rather than drop them — you get them back when you return, instead of a dialog
asking whether you meant it. Cross-workspace history plumbing so navigation between workspaces is a
real route with real entries.

Losing someone's writing is the worst thing a writing app can do. Everything else is an
inconvenience; that one makes you stop trusting it, and you don't come back.

Also fixed the Reference Panel's Physical Description and Voice fields and its prose truncation,
added an Edit-in-Lore jump from the panel, and put the Writing Scene Guide on the mobile keyboard
toolbar.

files.name: 2026-09-02.md

frontmatter.title: The Chekhov ledger stopped guessing

files.body:
A gate about making the analysis tools stop pretending to be more certain than they are.

The Chekhov ledger pairs setups with payoffs — the gun on the wall in chapter one, fired in chapter
twelve. It had been inferring those pairs, which works until two setups look similar and it
confidently pairs the wrong ones. Now a payoff can name the exact setup it settles, picked from a
list, and the panel says which pairings I stated and which it guessed. It also reports them in the
order they appear in the book rather than the order it happened to process them, which sounds trivial
and was the difference between a useful list and a scrambled one.

Same principle in the continuity audit. It was flagging events as impossibly close together using
scenes that had no time of day recorded at all — inventing precision from missing data. It now grades
findings by how much it actually knows, and where several scenes conflict it reports the worst one
rather than the first one it stumbled into.

Also redrew the character arc as a real chart instead of an approximation, then immediately fixed it
distorting its own dots and labels when the container changed size.

Smaller things: the deaths section in the scene modal collapses, and you can carry the previous
scene's cast forward with one click instead of re-tagging six people who never left the room.

files.name: 2026-09-03.md

frontmatter.title: Dialogue attribution stopped counting names

files.body:
Two things today, and both were replacing a cheap approximation with something that actually reasons.

Magic systems got costs. A system can define a reserve — mana, stamina, whatever it is in your world
— and each time a scene invokes it, it says who used it and how much it drained. That produces a
track per character showing their reserve rising and falling through the book, and a check that fires
when someone spends more than they have. The rule I stuck to: it reports the recovery that actually
happened in the text, not the amount they theoretically should have regained. Where it had to infer
who was wielding something from whose viewpoint the scene is in, it marks that point as inferred
rather than quietly presenting a guess as a fact.

I also removed the tier escalation ladder I'd built earlier the same day. It imposed a structure on
magic systems that only suited the one I had in mind.

The second half: dialogue attribution. Working out who said a line had been done by seeing whose name
appeared nearby, which is barely better than a coin flip in a scene with three people in it. Replaced
with a cascade of real rules, tried in order of confidence. Everything downstream that claims to know
who's speaking now rests on that instead.

Then the beginning of bring-your-own-key AI support, so the rules engine can hand its genuinely
ambiguous lines to a model. Mostly a day of finding out which providers can be called from a browser
at all, and making failures say what actually went wrong instead of guessing from a status code.

files.name: 2026-09-04.md

frontmatter.title: AI that labels, never writes

files.body:
Shipped the AI work and wrote down the constraint that governs it: the model labels things, it never
generates prose. It gets the lines the rules engine honestly can't attribute and returns a name. It
never writes a sentence that ends up in my book, and it never returns a number I then present as a
measurement.

I recorded that as a standing rule rather than leaving it as an intention, because it's the sort of
thing that erodes one reasonable-sounding feature at a time. I deleted an AI prose feature back in
August for exactly this reason and I'd rather not relearn it.

Several releases across the day, and most of them were the same lesson: a failing run has to say what
failed. Early on it would report a generic error while the provider had sent a perfectly clear
explanation. A rate limit now reads as "not yet" rather than "broken", since those need completely
different responses from me. And you choose which chapters to run rather than paying for the whole
manuscript to answer a question about chapter three.

The other half of the day was analysis that needed the better attribution to be possible at all:
checking whether a character's dialogue matches the idiolect I recorded for them, ranking who
actually speaks to whom, and naming setups I forgot to mark so I can mark them with a click.

Two small parsing fixes I enjoyed: it was reading contractions as quote marks, and treating a
paragraph's several quoted lines as one utterance.

Also added a daily word goal that survives having the app open in two tabs.

files.name: 2026-09-05.md

frontmatter.title: Rebuilt the plot timeline as a thread chart

files.body:
Two releases of the Story Planner and Timeline overhaul today, v2.43.0 and v2.44.0.

The first gate was mostly about admitting a feature hadn't worked. The Snowflake Wizard was meant to
walk you from a one-line premise up to a full outline, and in practice nobody finished it — you'd get
three steps in and abandon it. I pulled it out and replaced it with eleven starter Jots you can pick
up in any order, or ignore entirely.

Two follow-ups from that, both small and both my own fault:

- The starter Jots inherited copy from the wizard that promised automation they don't do. Writing a
  cheque the feature can't cash is worse than saying nothing.
- "Add Starter Jots" was confirming through a dialog whose primary button was a red *Delete*. It had
  been that way for a while, which is the part that bothers me — I'd looked straight past it more
  than once.

The second gate was the interesting one. Plot threads can now branch and merge, which meant the
timeline could no longer be drawn as a set of parallel lines. Redrew it as a proper thread chart
where a branch visibly leaves its parent and a merge visibly rejoins.

That surfaced a real bug rather than a cosmetic one. The code that works out the shape could be
handed a cycle — threads that eventually loop back into each other — and the cycle-breaking picked an
essentially arbitrary edge to cut, so the same project could render a different shape between runs.
Now it demotes the thread that closes the ring specifically, which is both stable and the answer a
reader would expect.

Non-determinism in a rendering path is the kind of bug that wastes a whole afternoon later,
because you can't reproduce it on demand. Worth the detour.

files.name: 2026-09-06.md

frontmatter.title: Jots stopped belonging to the account

files.body:
Finished moving Jots — the loose-notes workspace — from living on your account to living inside a
project, and cleaned up the bug that move exposed.

The bug: switching projects silently threw away whatever you typed next. The workspace would keep
showing the old project's note under the new project's name, and your next keystroke got saved to
an address that no longer existed. In one mode that write is quietly discarded, in the other it's
rejected. Either way the writing is gone and nothing tells you. That's the worst class of bug this
app can have, so the rule for what should be selected after a switch came out of the workspace and
into its own tested piece — it has a trap in it, two projects can coincidentally hold notes with
the same id, and the old code trusted that.

Then the migration for anyone who already had notes from before the move: ask once, pick which
project the old notes belong to, move them in, done.

Two smaller things I'd been walking past. Creating a project dropped you on an empty workspace — a
blank page is a question the app should answer, not ask, so new projects now arrive with starter
notes and the Read Me open. And the "Add Starter Jots" button was clickable when there was no
project to add them to.

Also set up this log. From here every session writes the day's entry as the work happens rather
than at the end, and the rules live in the repo so I don't have to keep repeating them. I'd asked
for the folder to be called `logs`; the format contract says `log`. The contract wins.

## Later — finishing it

Notes now travel with a project's backup. Leaving them out was right while they belonged to the
account, and wrong the moment they didn't — a backup that quietly drops every note in a project
isn't a backup.

Then the thing I only found by opening the migration screen myself instead of trusting the report
on it, and it's the same shape as the switch bug: a failure hiding behind a success message. If a
note failed to move it was skipped, the migration marked itself finished anyway, and that note was
stranded with the prompt never coming back. The likely cause is a note too long for the database to
swallow in one piece — exactly the kind of note I write. It now refuses to finish unless every note
lands, and says which didn't.

I checked all this in a browser before shipping, but against a fake account rather than my own. The
migration asks once which project your old notes belong to, and running it for real would have
answered that question for me. Not my call to make.

Shipped as v2.46.0.

Cut v2.46.1 straight after, with nothing in it. Two sessions had been committing to this repo at
once today and I wanted certainty rather than a reassurance that neither had left work stranded.
Checking said everything was already pushed and the only commits after the release were log entries,
so the running app was current either way — but "I checked and it's fine" is worth less than a tag
you can point at. An empty release is a cheap way to buy that.


## Later still — the chapter kept jumping to the top

Writing on the phone had a habit that finally annoyed me enough to chase: leave the app for
under a minute, come back, and the chapter you were in the middle of was scrolled back to its
first line. Your cursor was still exactly where you left it — tap once and you're typing in the
right place — but you had to scroll a thousand words to see what you were typing.

It turned out not to be about backgrounding at all. When the keyboard comes up, the prose box
stops being an ordinary block on the page and becomes its own little scrolling window, pinned
between the header and the toolbar so the writing area gets its height back on a small screen.
That swap is deliberate and I like it. What nobody had thought about is that a scrolling box
that has just come into existence starts at the top, and nothing ever moved it. Every keyboard
down-and-up did it; backgrounding was just the easiest way to trigger one. The reverse was
broken too — put the keyboard away and the page underneath was near the top, because the box
had been covering it and nobody was watching where it sat.

The fix is to notice which thing is doing the scrolling right now and put the cursor back about
a third of the way down it, in both directions. A third rather than the middle because it leaves
the paragraphs you just wrote on screen, which is the context you actually want.

The awkward part is that the box keeps growing while the keyboard slides in, so one correction
gets measured against a box that isn't finished yet — it has to keep re-checking until the size
holds still. And it has to know when to get out of the way: the moment you scroll it yourself,
put a finger on it, or type a character, it stops. A helpful nudge that fights you is worse than
no nudge.

That fixed the case where the app was still running. It doesn't help when the phone actually
kills it, or the tab reloads, or you come back the next morning — then the cursor is genuinely
gone and the chapter opens at the top with nothing to put back. So the position is now written
down, per device, and restored when you reopen the chapter. Four hundred milliseconds after the
cursor settles, and immediately whenever you leave: switching chapters, tapping out of the prose,
or the phone shoving the app into the background, which on a phone is usually the last thing that
happens before it gets killed.

I decided against syncing this to the account. It would mean a write on every sentence, and where
you stopped on your phone is rarely where you want to resume on a laptop — it's a device habit,
not a fact about the manuscript. Fifty chapters are remembered, oldest forgotten first, and the
whole thing is treated as untrusted on the way back in: it's storage a user can edit and it
outlives deploys, so a garbled entry has to be a shrug rather than a crash. A position past the
end of a chapter that's since been trimmed lands at the end.

It places the cursor and stops there — it doesn't open the keyboard. iOS won't do that without a
tap anyway, and an app that starts typing at you before you've asked is obnoxious on a laptop too.

Two things I got wrong in the first pass and only saw while wiring this up. The correction knew to
stand down when you typed, but not when something else moved the cursor — so a jump to a scene or
a search result would land, and then half a second later the earlier correction would drag the
view back to where the cursor used to be. And the cleanup on leaving the workspace was starting a
correction nobody would ever stop; harmless in practice because it times out, but it worked by
accident rather than on purpose. Both now say what they mean.

Checked both halves in a browser at a phone width before shipping: with the cursor left in the
middle of a long chapter, closing and reopening the keyboard now lands it a third of the way down
the box instead of at the top, and after a hard reload the chapter reopens exactly where it was —
with the cursor waiting there rather than the keyboard springing up. Shipped as v2.47.0.

## Killing the health strip

Deleted the row of count chips across the top of the Analysis Hub. It had ten tabs' worth of
numbers in it — unpaid plants, continuity errors, uncosted invocations — each one clicking through
to the tab that explains it.

I built it because ten tabs with no landing surface felt unfriendly: nothing told you what needed
attention without visiting each tab and already knowing what it was for. That reasoning was fine
and the thing I built to satisfy it was still wrong, because the Hub already has a landing surface.
It's called Overview and it's the first tab. So the strip was a second front door in front of the
first one, and it charged rent: it sat above the tab row on *every* tab, so a chunk of vertical
space went to duplicate numbers no matter which one you were reading. On a phone that's most of
what you can see at once. Every count it showed is still computed and still displayed by the tab
that owns it, so removing it loses nothing except the copy.

What made it interesting is what fell out. The Hub's tab row is icon-only below 768px, and I'd
justified that at the time by pointing at the chips right above it — the labels are there, just one
row up. Which means the strip I was about to delete was the only thing telling a phone user what
those ten icons were. Ten unlabelled icons is not a navigation bar, it's a puzzle.

So the tabs got their labels back at every width. They can't share the row equally anymore now that
they have text in them, so the row scrolls sideways instead — which is exactly what the chip row
did, so the gesture is one a user of this screen already had. Desktop is untouched.

Small lesson I keep relearning: a feature that's quietly propping up another one won't announce
itself. You find out when you pull it.

Checking the scrolling row in a browser turned up the thing I hadn't thought about: which tab you're
on is remembered globally, but where the row is scrolled to isn't. Leave the Hub on one of the last
tabs, come back, and the row is back at the start with the highlight sitting off-screen — so the
screen reads as having nothing selected. That's worse on a phone but it isn't a phone bug; a 1440px
window overflows too. The row now scrolls the selected tab into view on arrival and on every change,
at every width.

One more thing the release check caught, and it's the failure shape I keep finding: something
half-landing with nothing to announce it. The write-up of this change went into the reference doc
but never made it into the Help panel inside the app, because the compiled copy had been mistaken
for leftover clutter in the working folder and left behind. Nothing errors when that happens —
the doc is right, the app quietly says something older. My own build had muddied the water enough
to make the mistake reasonable, which is the part worth remembering: the check is to look at the
file, not to work out whose it was.

Shipped as v2.48.0.

files.name: 2026-09-08.md

frontmatter.title: The day I stopped guessing at Google

files.body:
I want to point the app at my Google Docs and have them turn up as notes, kept in step as I edit
them. There's a plan for it that runs to six phases, and all six rested on assumptions nobody had
checked. Two sittings today, both spent replacing a guess with a measurement.

The first assumption was about permissions. Google's cheap permission level is per-file — you get
what the user hands you through the picker and nothing more. What isn't documented is what happens
when the thing handed over is a *folder*. Does that reach the files inside, or just the folder? The
permission level that would settle it outright needs a formal security assessment, which is absurd
for a personal app. So I built the smallest possible thing that answers the question and nothing
else.

The answer is no. Picking a folder grants you the folder and its contents stay invisible. Asking
for them doesn't even fail — you get a perfectly cheerful empty list, which is the worst way to be
told no. Two false starts before I could trust that, both mine: the screen first reported success
on an empty result because I'd written the check to treat "no error" as "it worked", and then the
pick wasn't registering at all because I'd left out a parameter the picker needs to record the
grant, having read it as optional. For about an hour I had an answer that looked much worse than
the truth. Rather than take the failure at face value I tested the fallback in the same sitting:
picking documents individually works, and the permission grows by exactly what you picked. The
feature survives, one shape smaller — you choose documents rather than a folder, and adding one
later is a deliberate act rather than something that happens by itself.

The second sitting was the piece that turns a Google Doc into a note, and the same lesson landed
again. I had already guessed twice at what a Docs export looks like and been wrong both times, so
this time I exported a real chapter and read it. Three things in there would have quietly wrecked
my research. Most of the formatting markers say *nothing is applied here* — 29 of 41 — so a
converter that emphasises anything carrying a marker bolds the entire document. Runs of text split
mid-word, so joining them with a space sprinkles "two w eeks" through prose nobody re-reads line by
line. And every link is wrapped in a Google tracking redirect, so unprocessed, each cited source
points back at Google with a timestamp attached. Tables can't survive at all — the editor has no
notion of one — so each row becomes a line with the cells separated by pipes: content kept, grid
honestly lost.

The rest is rules about what a sync may do. It never overwrites a note I've edited, never deletes
one because a file went missing, and never fetches a document that hasn't changed. There's a
version stamp folded into the fingerprints so improving the converter later re-does the notes
instead of declaring every one of them conflicted forever.

Also found the throwaway test screen was unreachable but still being shipped, keys and all — the
bundler doesn't drop code just because nothing can reach it. Unreachable and absent aren't the same
thing.

files.name: 2026-09-09.md

frontmatter.title: The whole Drive feature, and three ways it could have eaten my prose

files.body:
Seven sittings and two releases, and the thing I set out to build a couple of days ago is done: my
research in Google Drive turns up in the app as notes and keeps itself current, a note that's
changed on both sides hands me the decision instead of picking for me, and any file on this machine
can become a note without Google being involved at all.

The only test I actually cared about all day was one I ran by hand. Edit a note here, edit the same
document in Drive, sync. If the app had quietly taken Drive's version, the whole feature would have
been a liability dressed up as a convenience. It stopped, said the note had been edited in both
places, and left my words alone.

Which is the theme of the day, really. Almost everything hard was a way this could have destroyed
something without ever telling me, and three of them nearly shipped. The sync works out that I've
deleted a note by not finding it in the list it was handed — perfectly correct until the list hasn't
loaded yet, at which point every mirrored document looks deleted and stops syncing for good,
silently. The background permission check was set to an option I was sure meant "don't show
anything", and it actually means "skip the consent screen if they've already agreed" — so the app
would have thrown a Google popup at me roughly hourly, unprompted. And the worst one arrived through
the button built to prevent exactly this: pressing "keep mine" has to convince the next sync there's
nothing left to do, but there are *two* separate reasons it can decide a note needs rewriting, and
clearing one and not the other makes the button look like it worked and then overwrites the words I
just chose to keep, five minutes later, with nothing on screen. There's a test now that starts in
that state and insists the next sync does nothing at all.

None of those would have failed loudly. That's what makes them worth the paranoia — a crash you find
in a minute; a note quietly replaced overnight you find in a month, if ever. The same instinct runs
through the rest of it: the access token is never written down anywhere, none of the Drive
bookkeeping goes into a backup, and keeping my own version asks Google when the document actually
changed rather than guessing, refusing to resolve at all if it can't reach it.

The smaller feature took an hour because the hard part already existed. Point at a Markdown file, a
Word document or a saved web page and it becomes a note, formatting intact, no account and no
network needed. One rule in there is invisible and would produce garbage backwards: Markdown has to
become markup *before* the sanitiser sees it, or every heading and bullet collapses into one grey
slab that looks almost right until you read it. I'd learned that on the Drive side already, so this
time there's a test that fails the moment anyone removes the step. An imported note is deliberately
just a note — no pretend link back to a file nothing is watching.

Two things about writing it all down. Documenting a feature forces you to notice what it doesn't do,
and three honest limitations went into the docs that I'd been comfortably not saying out loud — then
a day later two of them stopped being true and I had to go back and fix a limitations list that was
now *underselling* the thing, which is exactly as untrustworthy as one that oversells it. And I'd
been filing each sitting as its own dated file, so one day had four. That's not a daily log, that's
four fragments of a Tuesday. Merged them and changed the rules so it doesn't happen again; the
format always allowed either shape, so this was my own habit drifting rather than a spec problem.

Left undone on purpose: it only syncs while I'm actually looking at my notes, and nothing syncs with
the app closed. There's no server to receive Google's nudge, and there isn't going to be one.

files.name: 2026-09-17.md

frontmatter.title: Tidying the Plot Timeline, then chasing one wrong diagnosis into three

files.body:
Opening the Plot Timeline, the first thing you saw was three stacked boxes of settings and, somewhere underneath if you scrolled, the chart. Most of the page spent on controls I touch once a month, guarding the one view I came to look at. So they're three buttons on one row now, each opening *over* the chart rather than above it, with a badge so a shut panel still tells you what it's doing. On a phone they're the usual back-dismissible drawers — and checking that at phone width turned up the day's small bug, a thread-name box that refused to shrink and scrolled its drawer sideways.

Then the long part. I'd been sure the timeline didn't draw branches, because my threads showed as flat parallel lines. First answer: the feature's broken. Wrong. Second answer: the feature's fine and my data's empty, every thread top-level. Also wrong — two of my threads *are* branches of the main one, properly saved; I'd just never named the scene where each splits off, and the chart treated half-configured as not configured. So an unset branch now peels off at the thread's own first scene.

Which drew the branches, and then floated half my scenes off their own lines. The curve climbs over about a chapter, so starting it at the first scene meant every dot in that chapter sat at the thread's height above a line still rising out of its parent. Now the climb gets its run-up *before* the first dot, and a branch I've set myself doesn't move at all.

I wrote that fix up as a spec and got it wrong a third time — demanded a fixed run-up that a one-chapter book can't give, which would have yanked every deliberate branch to the left edge. Caught before it shipped, and there's a test pinning it now. Three wrong answers, each one comfortable, each one looking identical on the board. That's the thing worth remembering.

files.name: 2026-09-22.md

frontmatter.title: Drive out, prose follows the card, and exports finally show their blanks

files.body:
Five releases today, each one building on the last, and all of them about making the plan and the manuscript agree with each other.

Google Drive came back out of Jots. I did it as a removal on top of everything since, not a rewind, because three rounds of Plot Timeline work had landed after it.

Then the scene download, which had fallen behind the card. I rewrote it to walk the card top to bottom and pull in the scene's actual manuscript text. Review caught two slips: the word count counted markdown symbols as words, and End Scene marked a scene Drafted even when its break failed to land.

The part I cared most about was the planner. Dragging a scene to another chapter used to move the plan and leave its prose behind. Now every move carries the prose too, reorders included. A scene that was never ended moves its card only, because guessing prose boundaries from `* * *` breaks is how you mangle a novel. There's no confirmation dialog. Each chapter it touches gets a Version History snapshot first, and that's the undo.

Last, the exports. A field with no value used to be silently missing, so I couldn't tell "blank" from "not included". Every field now prints, and the empty ones are marked as empty. Chasing that turned up something worse: the chapter download had never been rewritten at all and was still printing the old thin summary. My mistake. I'd treated the card's download and the chapter's as one thing. It now embeds every scene in full, in card order. Review then caught one more slip before it went out: the whole-project export had lost every scene's name. Fixed, and live.

files.name: 2026-09-23.md

frontmatter.title: One scene, many setups: plants and payoffs become a list

files.body:
A scene can now plant and pay off as many things as it actually does, not one. Real scenes don't work one setup at a time. The gun goes on the wall in the same scene the letter goes in the drawer, and a good climax settles both. The planner only ever let me record one of them, so the other lived in my head, which is exactly where a Chekhov ledger is supposed to stop things living.

The scene modal now has a Plants & Payoffs list that works like System Invocations: add a plant, add a payoff, and each row gets its own thread and note. When a payoff picks what it settles, it picks a specific plant, not a scene. A scene that planted three things shows up three times in the picker, by name. The ledger counts each one on its own, so one scene can have a setup that's paid and another that's still owed.

I didn't migrate anything. Old scenes are read as a one-item list, and saving one quietly switches it over. The one tricky part was old payoff links. They pointed at a scene, back when a scene held one plant at most. They now mean that scene's first plant, which is what they always meant. They get pinned to that exact plant the next time you open the payoff, so adding a second plant later can't shift the pairing.

Doing this turned up a real bug in the AI plant suggestions. Accepting one on a scene that already paid something off threw the payoff away and put the plant in its place. That was my mistake, and it's been there since the feature shipped. Now the plant is added next to the payoff. The suggestions still skip any scene that already has a plant marked. Opening that up means changing what the model is asked, so I'll decide it on its own.

Shipped as v2.57.0 and it's live. Types, tests and build are clean, but I haven't clicked through it in a browser yet, on desktop or phone. That comes next, against real scenes.

files.name: 2026-09-25.md

frontmatter.title: The Markdown downloads stop falling behind

files.body:
Downloading a book, a chapter or a character as Markdown had quietly fallen behind the app. Today I caught it up, and made sure it can't drift again.

Character and lore downloads were the worst. Links to other entries printed as long internal ids, custom fields and field history never reached the file, and blank fields were dropped, so a field that had stopped exporting looked exactly like one you'd never filled in. That's on me: the exporter was written months ago, and every field since depended on someone remembering to add it. Nobody did. Now it reads the same field definitions the forms use, resolves links to names and prints every field, blanks marked. Checking that work caught one more: an unfilled number is stored as zero, so a character with no Enneagram type exported as "type 0".

The whole-book download's "include" toggles never did anything. They work now, and timeline events and project settings joined as sections.

Then a last sweep of loose ends. Switch a scene card from Scene to Sequel and the first set of answers hides but stays on the record, so it never reached the download. It now prints under a note. Old timeline events typed before the calendar existed lost their original wording, era name included; the file keeps it next to the computed date. The whole-book file's outline was upside down, every chapter and profile outranking the section it sat in. A heading you typed into a chapter or a character's backstory did the same, landing at the very top of the outline; now it sits under its section. And the character form had the Maslow picker labelled "Tension Level".

The part I care about most is a new test: every field of every record has to reach its download or carry a written reason why not, and a new field fails the build until it does. Remembering didn't work, so now the build remembers.

Before shipping I clicked through every download in a browser, at desktop and phone width, on a throwaway copy rather than my real book. That pass is what found the typed-heading problem. It shipped as v2.58.0.

files.name: 2026-10-10.md

frontmatter.title: The scene graph was lying about flashbacks, so I replaced it with a Story Map I can scroll along and read

files.body:
I opened the Scene Chronology graph on my actual book today and it told me nothing. By the end of the day it was gone from the tab and a Story Map I can scroll along was sitting there instead, unreleased and not yet looked at in a browser.

The old graph was a column of unlabelled dots, and its one headline claim was false: the diagonal meant to mark a story told in order only held for a story paced perfectly evenly. That was a mistake in the design, so it gets replaced, not patched.

The Story Map runs the story across in lanes, under a ribbon of dates. Order is plotted against order, and it says the telling "steps back in time", never "flashback"; two storylines told in alternation step back constantly without either being one.

The first cut fitted the whole book to the screen, and with 64 scenes every one was a dot. So now it opens zoomed in just far enough to read and moves sideways only, under wheel, drag, pinch and arrow keys, over a strip showing the whole book.

Then it had to be readable, which it wasn't. The ribbon had one way to write a date, the full one, which needs about 95 pixels in a column 22 wide, so where the tab opens it said nothing at all. Each day now says as much as fits: the full date, the day and month, or the bare number, with a heavier edge where the month turns and the month named at the left. Pills carry their titles where their lane is clear beside them, and pointing at a scene shows a card at once and lights up every scene of its colour.

The worst bug was the first click. Selecting a scene opens a detail column, which narrows the chart, and the view kept the same scenes in less room, so every pill turned into a dot. A resize now keeps the scale and shows fewer scenes.

Calls worth recording.

A scene with a date and no time is not a midnight scene. Read that way, "13 July" looks like a jump backwards after a ten-at-night scene the same day.

A press on a scene stays a tap until it has travelled sideways. Taking hold of the pointer sooner would have sent every tap's click to the chart instead.

Two mistakes were mine. I asked for colours that read "on the dark background" without saying which dark, and four failed on the real one. And I said the readability work would rewrite one existing test; it rewrote four, one of which had only ever passed because of the tooltip being removed.

None of it has been felt on a phone or seen at real font sizes yet. Still to come: filters, and a corrected version of the old graph beside it.

files.name: 2026-10-11.md

frontmatter.title: The Story Map shipped: titles, filters, an honest Curve, and room to fill the screen

files.body:
Four things happened to the Story Map today: most scenes turned out to have no title on a book shaped like mine, the map got its filters, the old scatter graph came back as a second view that tells the truth, and the whole thing can now be maximised.

**Titles.** The report said thirty-three of thirty-five scenes carried a title. That was measured on a made-up book whose scenes hop lanes every time. Real plot threads run for several scenes in a row, and on a book like mine ten of thirty-five had one. Titles now take turns above and below their scene, and thirty-four show.

**Filters.** Chapters, points of view, threads, locations and statuses can be chosen from a column, a drawer on a phone, or the legend.

**The Curve.** The graph this rebuild replaced plotted in-world time against reading order, with a diagonal for a story told in order. The new view plots order against order: told straight through is the diagonal, a flashback is visibly off it. Then I deleted the old graph.

**Maximise.** A button fills the window with the map; on a phone it becomes a full-screen pane, and Back puts it away. Escape restores. My first rule for it was wrong: it ignored Escape in every input, checkboxes included, so after ticking a filter it did nothing. It now yields only to controls you type into. The scene detail finally says where the scene is, "12 of 61 shown, story order 9 of 40", with Previous and Next to walk from there. It also used to sit open, saying nothing, for a scene the filters had taken off the map. Now it says so.

Opening a scene in the Manuscript from the phone's sheet never closed the sheet; it lingered in the Back stack. It closes first now.

**Shipped.** Until this evening none of it had been seen in a browser. It has now, on a sixty-scene book at desktop and phone size, and it went out as v2.59.0. The day's lesson is still about tests: a fixture tidier than real data will pass anything.

files.name: 2026-10-19.md

frontmatter.title: Gate A held up; planning the Story Map's second axis, story time

files.body:
After a week of writing with the new Story Map I'm happy with it, so the next stage has started: laying scenes out by when they happen in the world, not just the order I tell them in.

That turned out to be a bigger change than the plan made it look. Everything under the map, from zooming and panning to the minimap and the arrow keys, assumes the axis is counted in scenes, one equal column each. Story time is counted in minutes. So the work is three pieces rather than one: the arithmetic first, tested on its own, then the drawing, then the controls.

I made four calls before any code. A scene with no recorded length gets a short fixed mark, not a made-up one-hour bar, because a chart that invents data is worse than one with gaps. A scene dated to a day but with no time is spread across its part of the day in reading order and marked as a guess, rather than all of them piling up at midnight. By default every run of empty days collapses into one labelled break, with a toggle for true scale. And most of my scenes already have dates, times and lengths, so overlapping bars are the normal case and the stacking has to be right, not an afterthought.

One bug got folded in too: a scene with an hour outside 0-23, which can only come from imported or hand-edited data, was landing on the next day.

No code today, only the plan and the first brief.

files.name: 2026-11-13.md

frontmatter.title: Story time, before any of it is drawn: the maths under the second axis

files.body:
Today I built the arithmetic for laying the Story Map out by when things happen in the world. None of it draws anything yet. That was on purpose: every claim the chart will make has a test behind it first.

The idea is simple: every scene sits where it happens, as a bar as long as it lasts. The details are where it gets hard. Most of my book has dates, times and lengths, so overlapping bars are the normal case, and each storyline stacks its overlaps into rows. Those rows are worked out over the whole book, never over what's on screen, so panning can't reshuffle them. Empty stretches between busy days fold into one narrow break, however long they are, and the month labels honour that: a break that skips March, April and May gets a single "May" where the story picks up again, not three labels on one spot.

A scene dated to a day but given no time now gets spread across whatever part of the day is left. That's between the scene it follows and the next fixed time, in reading order. It's marked as a guess, not piled up at midnight.

The bug from the plan is fixed. A scene with an impossible hour, like 25 from imported data, was landing on the next day. I clamped it where the minute is first worked out, not just on the new axis, because otherwise the Curve and the time axis would disagree about when the same scene happens.

I also tried to break it on purpose. A typo'd scene a hundred million minutes long must not hang the tab, and three centuries drawn day by day must not build a hundred thousand labels just to throw them away. Both now count before they build. An absurdly long book gets squeezed to fit rather than cut off.

Three of my own test expectations were wrong today, all about calendars. Every time, the code was right and my head-maths wasn't. Day 65 really is the first of a month in a made-up calendar, whatever I thought.

Then I checked it independently, the way every piece of this gets checked: twelve hundred random books, two calendars, one of them deliberately lopsided, and every day label and month label compared against a slow walk through the calendar. They all agreed, and no stacked scenes overlapped. Next comes drawing it.

files.name: 2026-11-15.md

frontmatter.title: Story time gets drawn and switched on, trend strips go under the lanes, and the test failures that were never load

files.body:
The Story Map can now be laid out by when things happen in the world, with a switch for it in the toolbar and two thin trend strips under the lanes. Reading order is still the default. Story time is one click away, compressed or true scale.

Drawing it came first. Each dated scene is a bar as long as it lasts. A scene with no recorded length gets a small capsule, because a very short bar would lie about how long it took. Overlaps are normal in my book, so scenes stack into rows worked out over the whole book: panning can never shuffle a scene into a different row, and nothing is dropped.

Then the switch, and what I cared about was place: each way of looking remembers where you were. The arrow keys walk in time order, which means jumping from the end of a flashback straight into the present. Scenes with no date sit in a tray under the chart. Previous and Next in the detail card stay in reading order on purpose. They say "Scene 12 of 40", and changing that would be a lie.

The strips came last. One is a single tension line for the whole book, with a gap wherever I never set tension rather than a made-up middle value, and a dot for a lone value so it doesn't vanish. Across a break the line goes dashed, because the days between aren't drawn. Under story time a second strip shows the order I tell things in, tinted wherever the telling steps back. I left that one out of reading order, since the Curve already shows it. Each strip costs the lanes 28 pixels (24 on a phone), which can tip them into scrolling and narrow the plot, so the chart and the panel now share one sum for it and a test fails if they disagree.

Then I looked at it in a browser, on a test book and at phone size. Everything worked, but the telling strip was nearly useless. It was squeezed into about 20 pixels for the whole book, so each scene moved it less than a pixel and the flashback came out as one long flat pink line. Meanwhile the lanes left a big empty band beneath them. So before releasing, one small fix: the strips will grow into that empty space, and the telling line will scale to whatever is on screen.

One thing had been wrong for weeks. Every so often the whole test suite "failed" with no tests run, and I blamed a busy machine. It wasn't. Starting the tests from the terminal that spells the drive letter in lower case makes the runner load itself twice. From the other terminal the same code passes every time.

files.name: 2026-11-16.md

frontmatter.title: Two Story Map releases in a day: story time as v2.60.0, then arcs, deaths, trails, world events and saved views as v2.61.0

files.body:
The second stage of the Story Map shipped today as v2.60.0, and by the end of the day the third and final stage had shipped too, as v2.61.0: arcs and deaths, following one character, the world's events along story time, and saved views.

The release needed one fix first: the trend strips were squashed while a short book left hundreds of pixels empty below them, and a flashback barely moved the telling line in a long book. Now the strips use the spare room.

Arcs and deaths came in three steps: the arithmetic, the drawing, the wiring. The map doesn't pair plants and payoffs itself; it reads them off the Chekhov ledger, with tests that fail if the two ever disagree. The detail card finally says what a scene plants and who dies in it, which I promised at the first stage and never delivered. That was my planning mistake, not the build's.

A Follow picker draws a line through every scene one character is in and fades the rest. It stops at their death, but a scene where I deliberately tagged them back in stays bright. A flashback told after they die and set before it is still cut. I could be argued out of that.

The Event Lanes events now show as diamonds on the story-time band. Under reading order I draw nothing rather than put an event somewhere false.

Last, saved views. The map has so many settings now that a view worth finding is a view worth keeping. I can name the current setup and get it back in one click, viewport included. They stay on the device, per project: a handful of ids doesn't earn a sync. A saved view naming a chapter I've since deleted just drops it. One small fix rode along: a world event timed at hour 30 slid into the next day, and is now held to its own day the way scenes are.

Before releasing I ran it in a browser on a seeded book, desktop and phone, with nothing touching my real data. Everything worked. The trail reads clearly; the skull is crisp on a phone but only a small rose ring on a plain monitor, which I can live with because the cards name the death. A diamond still can't be tapped for its name on a phone. I checked it on my own book and signed it off, which closes the Story Map work that started in October.

files.name: 2026-11-17.md

frontmatter.title: The Scene Guide looked wrong on my phone: a few hundred classes that never existed, then a tidier layout

files.body:
I went to tidy the Writing Scene Guide on my phone because it looked cramped, and found something much bigger: a few hundred styling instructions across the whole app that have never done anything.

The guide was meant to have padding and gaps between its sections. It had neither, on any screen. The classes asking for them named a step the styling system doesn't have, and when it doesn't recognise one it quietly emits nothing. No error, no warning, no failed build. The finished stylesheet confirmed it: the rules simply weren't there.

Once I knew what to look for, it was everywhere, and had been since the initial import. Dozens of icons rendered at the default 24 pixels instead of the size I meant. Worse, the app is dark-only and the dark border colour on cards was one of the missing shades, so cards all over the app have had near-white outlines I'd stopped seeing.

I fixed it app-wide rather than patch one panel. Most of the missing steps were obviously meant to sit midway between two real ones, so I defined them as exactly that, and every existing class started working without being edited. A handful of plain typos I fixed by hand.

The part I care about most is the guard. A test now checks every colour shade and spacing step in the source against the real theme, and fails with a file-and-line list if one doesn't exist. It has to prove it can fail, and prove it looked at thousands of classes, because a check that matches nothing passes forever. Silent failures have bitten this repo again and again.

With the spacing real, the guide was still cluttered, so I reorganised it. POV, location, threads and beat share one row, and the tagged entities and the death list each fold into a collapsible section, closed by default. The death section keeps a red "recorded" badge on its header, because a closed section must never hide that someone died in the scene.

files.name: 2026-11-18.md

frontmatter.title: The Scene Guide fits on one line on my phone, and the styling fix ships as v2.62.0

files.body:
The tidied Scene Guide still wasn't right on my phone: with my real character names, the plot-thread chip fell onto its own line again, which was exactly what I'd set out to stop.

The row was only a little too wide, a dozen pixels or so, but that's enough to push the last chip down. The long POV name and the location name were doing most of the damage, and the "POV:" and "Loc:" labels in front of them were pure overhead. So on phones only, those two labels are now a small eye and a map pin. They keep their yellow and green colours, and a screen reader still hears the words. Desktop is untouched, and I left the Beat chip alone since it wasn't the problem.

Then I shipped yesterday's work and today's together as v2.62.0. Because the styling fix changes colours across the whole app, I went through every workspace first, in a throwaway copy with none of my real data. Panels that had been sitting flush against their edges have their padding back, and the borders are finally the quiet grey they were always meant to be. The dimmer grey text I'd worried would be hard to read never actually shows: everywhere it's used, something brighter already wins.

One thing I'm not pretending away: two of the Story Map's tests time out when the whole suite runs at once. They pass on their own and nothing today touched them, so it's a flaky time limit rather than a broken map. But a test that fails sometimes is a test people learn to ignore, so it's next on the list.

files.name: 2026-11-19.md

frontmatter.title: Writing down what this project taught me, before I start the next one

files.body:
No code today. I'm about to start a new project, so I sat down to turn three months of rules, written here one breakage at a time, into a single starting file I can carry into anything.

Most of what's in it isn't about this app at all. The biggest lesson is the shape of the bugs that actually hurt. Almost every serious one silently dropped something, inflated something, or served something stale, with no error anywhere: a field that stopped exporting and looked exactly like an empty one, a test guard that matched nothing and so always passed, a deploy that went to the wrong project and reported success. A crash gets found in a minute. Those get found in a month, so the new file tells whoever works on it to hunt for that shape on purpose.

The rest is how I work now, rather than how I started. Every model change reaches every export in the same commit, and the build enforces it, because remembering didn't work. A worker session's report is a claim to check, not a result to believe. Nobody quotes a line number from memory, because a made-up one feels exactly like a real one. Browser automation gets one try before I take over by hand.

Then I did the same for the brief I paste into every planning session. The new one gives every plan the same skeleton, including what I deliberately chose not to do and what the next step has to fold in. Every brief now ends by asking the worker where it didn't match the code, because workers have caught my mistakes that way more than once.

Writing it also showed me which of my old rules had gone stale. The model guidance and the editor notes no longer matched how I actually work, so they're gone from the new version.

frontmatter.title: Budget app: from research doc to a build plan, an empty project that builds, colours I can trust, money that adds up, one definition for every record, a first place to keep it, transfers that can't lose money, a test run that is fast again, a database that turns away anyone not invited, a data layer ready for the cloud, and a cloud branch that keeps working offline

files.body:
I started a new project today: a free budgeting app for me, my family and people I invite, built for how money actually moves in Ghana, with mobile money first and cedis by default, and nothing behind a paywall.

The day began with research. I went through how the big apps (YNAB, Monarch, Copilot, PocketGuard, Actual and others) do things, what people love about them and why they quit. The research also turned up hard limits. Bank linking in Ghana isn't live yet. Google Play won't let an app read SMS. Every per-user service, such as bank data, AI or email, costs money I'm not spending yet. I answered all seventeen open decisions in one go: everything free, nothing paid built yet, paste-in SMS instead of reading it, Flex budgeting as the default, one installable web app first, and invite-only until I've registered with the Data Protection Commission.

Then I picked the stack. It's the same React-and-Firebase setup I already know, on the free plan only. That means no server functions, so things like the invite list have to be enforced by the database rules themselves. I'm designing for phones first, because that's where people here handle their money.

The first release is deliberately narrow: sign in, add your accounts, record spending in three taps, and see one honest "safe to spend" number that never counts money I haven't received yet. It also has to work offline. Everything else, from SMS paste to forecasting, waits for later releases. Every other app I looked at was weakest exactly where it tried to do everything at once.

By the end of the day the empty project builds, lints and tests, with one placeholder screen. I kept TypeScript on 6.0 on purpose, because the linter doesn't support 7 yet and I'd rather not fight my tools on day one.

I also set up the colours for light and dark, and added a test that asks the styling tool whether every class in the code is real. On my last project, made-up style classes shipped for weeks and quietly did nothing; now a typo can no longer silently do nothing. Then I found the new guard had a bug of its own: it could call a correct class wrong depending on which test ran first, and it couldn't see classes chosen by an if. The flaw was in my plan, not in the code that followed it, so I fixed the plan's design and made the guard refuse any class value it can't read. A second test checks that the colours stay readable in both themes, and overspending shows as amber, not red, because it isn't an emergency.

Last came the rules for money and dates, before any screen needs them. Every amount is stored as whole pesewas, never as a fraction, because computers can't hold 0.1 exactly: add 0.1 and 0.2 and you get 0.30000000000000004, and those slivers pile up in a running balance. The amount box will work as a small calculator, so "45+12.5" just works. Commas only count as thousands separators. If someone types "12,5" meaning twelve and a half, I'd rather refuse it than quietly record 125. A late-night entry stays on the day it happened in your own time zone.

Then the money step's own worker caught a hole I'd written into the plan. I'd said to strip all spaces before reading an amount, so "12 5" became 125 and "1 250" became 1,250: exactly the silent misreading the comma rule exists to stop. The fault was my rule, not the code. Now a space inside a number is refused, and a typed amount is capped at 100 characters, because a few thousand nested brackets used to crash the reader instead of just saying no.

The last step today gave every record the app will store, from accounts and categories to transactions and budget months, one definition, with a plain name for each field and a check that runs before anything is saved. "Not planned" and "planned zero" are now different things that can never be confused, and a category nobody has sorted isn't quietly counted as Flex. The worker also caught a contradiction in my plan: I'd asked for a test record of a transaction with every field filled in to pass, but no real transaction can be a transfer and have a category at the same time. The plan was wrong, not the code, so the test now says plainly which fields depend on each other and why.

Then the app got somewhere to keep things. For now that's the browser itself, so accounts, categories and my profile can be saved and read back before the cloud database exists. I cared more about how it fails than how it works. A save that breaks a rule, or hits a full browser, leaves everything exactly as it was. If the saved data can't be read, the app stops and says so instead of quietly starting fresh, because starting fresh means deleting everything I'd typed. An account's currency also locks once it has transactions, so changing cedis to dollars can't silently reinterpret every amount in it. Along the way I tightened three checks the last step had let through: ids the cloud database would reject later, blank notes passing as real ones, and an icon limit too short for a single family emoji.

By evening money could actually be recorded: spending, income, transfers, balance corrections and budget months. A transfer is saved, changed and deleted as one, so it can never leave one half behind and make money appear or vanish. I checked that with ten thousand entries, and every balance and every currency total came out to the pesewa. A balance correction records only the difference between what the app thinks and what my wallet says, and nothing at all when they agree. Two things I'm not proud of turned up. The id maker I'd carried over had been producing ids that weren't quite the standard shape on phones without a secure connection. And because every save rewrites everything in browser-only mode, saving slows as the history grows. That's fine for testing, but it's no way to keep a real year of spending.

Late in the day I noticed the full test run had crept up to about three minutes, and that was my fault: I had specified one test as ten thousand separate saves, and every save in browser-only mode rewrites everything, so it got slower with every record. Nobody runs a three-minute suite, so it would have been skipped or ignored. The checks that matter are the same: ten thousand records, every transfer whole, every balance and currency total exact. But the bulk is now stored in one go, and a couple of hundred real saves then have to keep it reconciled. The whole suite runs in well under a minute. The same pass closed two ways to strand your own entries: moving an account's starting date past entries already in it, and switching a category between spending and income while entries or a budget month still use it. Neither gave an error at the time, and both would have shown up weeks later as an edit that refused for no visible reason. One of my older tests had been doing exactly the first thing on purpose, so I rewrote it to expect the refusal.

The last step before the cloud database goes live was its rules, because on the free plan there's no server to stand guard, so the database has to do it alone. It now refuses anyone whose email isn't on my invite list, and nobody can add themselves to that list. A test proves one invited person can't read, list or touch another person's money: the request is refused outright, not quietly answered with nothing. I broke the rules on purpose to check the tests would notice, and they did. My first attempt at that check "failed" only because the test tool wasn't found, which would have passed for proof if I hadn't read the output.

The cloud branch can't wait for the server to answer before saying "saved", because offline it never answers. So before writing it I gave the app a way to hear about a refusal later, and a way to tell "you have nothing here" from "nothing has loaded on this device yet". The rules both versions of the data layer have to follow also moved into one place, so they can't quietly drift apart.

Then the cloud branch itself went in for my profile, accounts and categories. It says "saved" once the phone has the change, not once the server does, because on a bad mobile connection the server may not answer for hours, and a button that spins until then is a button nobody trusts. I tested it against the real access rules on a local copy of the database, including the awkward case where the phone accepts a change offline and the server refuses it later. That refusal now arrives as a message instead of the record quietly vanishing. Two edits made in quick succession to the same account both stick, because only the changed fields are sent. Breaking each of those on purpose made its test fail, so the tests aren't just passing. The tests also caught a trap I hadn't thought of: a starting balance of "minus zero" passed every check in the app, but the database stores it as a fraction, so the rules threw the new account away after the phone had already said it was saved. It's now written as a plain zero.

Before writing the cloud half for transactions, transfers and budget months, I moved the money rules (what a transfer's two halves must match, what a balance correction records, what can be planned) into the one place the cloud version will call, so it can't quietly apply different ones; nothing changed on screen and every existing test passed untouched.

frontmatter.title: Budget app: from first sign-in to a safe-to-spend number, a setup that gets you there, and an app that installs and works offline

files.body:
The app now does what it's for, from the first sign-in: a short setup gets a new person to a working Home, "+" records what you spent, and Home says what's safe to spend this month, with the sum behind it a tap away. It also installs to a phone's home screen and opens offline.

Sign-in fixed two things that would have looked like a broken app: someone not invited got saves that seemed to work and then quietly failed, and a Ghanaian phone set to "en-US" got Sunday weeks. The worst Accounts bug was quiet: another device renames an account while you have it open, you press Save without touching anything, and the old name goes back. Forms now send only what you changed.

Safe to spend is the smaller of the Flex budget left and the cash you actually have minus the bills still to pay, so it never says yes to money you don't have. Unsorted spending counts against Flex, and expected salary is planned with but never counted as cash.

The worst find came late. In cloud mode a save lands on the phone first, and if the cloud refuses it afterwards, the change is rolled back. Nothing in the app was listening, so the change just vanished without a word. Now a red banner says what was undone and why, and stays until you dismiss it.

Setup only appears for someone with no accounts and no categories, and the device remembers how far you got, so no profile field and no database rule changed. Updates never reload by themselves; a box asks first, because a reload mid-typing loses your work.

The test suite had crept to 57 seconds. The cause was the test tool's own ordering: the slowest file started last, and it kept rebuilding its fake browser whenever it switched between kinds of file. Fixing the order and giving five files one shared stand-in for the data layer brought it to about 39 seconds, with more tests. I also caught a flaky test I'd just written. None of this has been on a real phone yet.

frontmatter.title: Budget app: the first release went live, export jumped the queue, a new look, and entries learned to split and carry their fees

files.body:
The budget app's first release, v0.1.0, went live today: Google sign-in (invite only), a short setup, accounts, entries, categories, a Flex budget and a safe-to-spend number, installable and working offline. By night it could export my data, had a new look, and its entries could be split and carry their fees.

The browser pass before shipping caught a quiet one: Accounts said "Overdrawn, −30" while Home said 20, because Accounts counted an entry dated two days ahead. Both now use the balance as of today. My phone passed install, Back and airplane mode, so gate 1 is done.

Gate 2 opened with what I should have had from the start: a way out. My data sits on a free plan with no backups, so "Export my data" saves one zip. Then the look, which I'd called sooooo basic: white and navy, money in green and money out orange. Home now leads with a pace ring, tiles for what's over plan or unsorted, and money out each day.

Then the model underneath Ghana's money. One MoMo payment is often groceries plus airtime, so an entry can be split over categories, with parts that must add up to the pesewa. Entries also take tags and the SMS's transaction ID. And most MoMo transfers carry a fee on its own line, so a fee is now its own entry tied to the payment or transfer it was charged on: saved with it, moved when its date or account changes, deleted with it. The tie lives in the fee's own id, so deleting a payment takes its fee along even offline, without having to look the fee up first. Nothing can type any of this in yet; the form comes next.

Two fixes rode along. "Over by" stayed amber while my cash was below zero too, which hid real trouble; it's red now. And a test that failed once in ten turned out to answer a Back before the app had asked for one. Waiting for the ask fixed it.

frontmatter.title: Budget app v0.2.0: split payments, fees and tags, saved views, and pasted MoMo and bank messages read into an inbox

files.body:
Version 0.2.0 of the budget app went live tonight. The entry form now handles how money actually moves in Ghana: one MoMo payment split over groceries and airtime, the fee that came with it, and tags like "Trip to Kumasi". The list can be searched and saved as a named view, and pasting a day's MoMo and bank texts turns most of them into ready-to-confirm entries.

Two things I'd have shipped broken got caught early. A tag typed but not entered was silently thrown away on Save, and a saved view holding a tag nobody uses any more showed "Any" while still narrowing the list.

The SMS work came in two halves. First a To review inbox: a pasted message waits there and nothing touches a balance until I confirm it. A bank's one-time sign-in code is dropped before anything is saved, and a possible repeat is checked against both sides of a transfer, three days either way, because the bank posts late. Then the readers: MTN MoMo and GCB, built from my own redacted texts, pull out the amount, fee, date and transaction ID and match the message to an account by the last four digits of its number. MoMo texts carry no date, so those items are dated the day I paste them and say so.

Then random pastes caught a nasty one: a bank message pasted right before a sign-in code or a notice could vanish, counted as the code. My own tests only joined samples in the file's order, where it never happens. Now every pair is tested. One flaky cloud-database test stays open, and I didn't add a retry to hide it.

At release the test suite crept to 60 seconds on the same code that ran in 43 a few hours earlier. I didn't blame the laptop until I'd proved it: on a quiet machine it was 45 again. No browser pass this time, by my own choice. I went through the whole checklist on my phone instead, gate 1's leftovers included, and it all held, so gate 2 is done.
